newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto re-elected Japan P.M., to name cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto re-elected Japan P.M., to name cabinet.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was formally re-elected by Japan's parliament on Thursday on the strength of a loose alliance his party has formed with its old coalition partners.
Hashimoto was later due to name the 20-member cabinet in his new minority government.

Hashimoto garnered 262 votes in the premiership vote by parliament's main chamber, the 500-seat Lower House, against 152 for his closest rival, opposition leader Ichiro Ozawa, the house speaker said in announcing the result.
Hashimoto took a deep bow after his re-election was announced by House Speaker Soichiro Ito, amid a hail of applause from his party colleagues and allies.
The Upper House also voted to keep Hashimoto as prime minister.

But Hashimoto, 59, will govern at the head of a minority government after his conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) failed to win a majority in a general election last month and then failed to renew the outgoing coalition.
The LDP holds 239 seats in the Lower House, 12 short of a majority.
Instead of forming a coalition, the party's old allies, the Social Democrats and the Sakigake party, agreed to join a loose policy alliance with the LDP without taking part in the new cabinet.
That means Hashimoto's cabinet will be comprised entirely of LDP members, the first time in three years for the party to monopolise the cabinet.

Hashimoto was expected to keep Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda in his job because of a pressing foreign policy schedule, including key talks with Russia, China and the United States, parliamentary sources and media reports said.

Pending foreign policy issues include cementing a new security arrangement with the United States first announced in April by Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton, and mending ties with China marred by a row over disputed islands and Hashimoto's visit to a controversial war shrine.
Hashimoto was also expected to re-appoint Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama, an LDP stalwart who performs the twin roles of cabinet coordinator and top government spokesman.
On the domestic front, Hashimoto must tackle the vexed issue of streamlining a bloated and over-zealous bureaucracy, the first target being the towering Finance Ministry.

Thus the most important post in the new cabinet would be that of the finance minister, which was expected to be filled by Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, a former trade minister and leader of one of the factions that make up the LDP.

The new finance minister may preside over reforms that could sap the ministry's power by creating a separate body to oversee banks and other financial institutions, following scandals involving senior bureaucrats and alleged mishandling of Japan's financial woes.
News reports said Hashimoto has asked Shinji Sato, the son of Japan's longest-serving post-war prime minister, Eisaku Sato, as his new trade minister.
The new cabinet line-up was expected to include only one woman, Michiko Ishii, as the new environment minister.
